title: Terumah: the cherubim face each other (Exodus 25:20–22)
hook: two golden figures face one another, and God speaks from between them

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Terumah, the ark gilded inside and out. Your line was gold inside and out. What good thing did you do that nobody saw? Today, what stands on top of the ark. Day three hundred fifty-six.

Two people sit at a café table, both on their phones. Shoulders angled away, eyes down, the occasional mm-hm. A minute later, the phones go away. They turn toward each other, elbows on the table, and one of them says something true, and the other hears it. Same table. Different room entirely. On top of the ark, the Torah asks for a lid of pure gold, and on it two golden figures. The instructions say exactly which way they should face. And then God says where the voice will come from.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, TWO PHONES.` → `THEN THEY TURN TOWARD EACH OTHER.` → `TWO GOLDEN FIGURES.`

segments.voice: The figures are called keruvim, cherubim. Forget the chubby baby angels of Renaissance paintings; that picture came much later. In the Torah, keruvim are winged guardians. In Genesis, keruvim guard the way back to the garden of Eden. Here, two of them are hammered out of the same piece of gold as the lid of the ark, one at each end. Their wings spread upward, sheltering the lid, and the old Jewish translation says they stand "with their faces one to another." Then God tells Moses: there I will meet with thee, and speak with thee, "from between the two cherubim." Not from the gold. Not from either figure. From the space between two faces turned toward each other. The Talmud has an odd and lovely detail. One sage says keruv sounds like the Aramaic for like a child, and so the cherubim had young faces. And it notices a problem. In the book of Chronicles, the cherubim in Solomon's Temple face the house, not each other. Which is it? The Talmud answers: when Israel does God's will, they face each other. When not, they turn away. The faces show the state of the relationship. Read mystically or not, the picture holds. Something holy can happen in the space between two people who are really facing one another. That space is where this text says the voice comes from.
screen: `KERUVIM: WINGED GUARDIANS.` · `FACES ONE TO ANOTHER.` · `FROM BETWEEN THE TWO CHERUBIM.` · `FACING, OR TURNED AWAY.` · then, large: `THE VOICE BETWEEN THE FACES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture turning toward someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person you'll talk with today. A partner, a child, a coworker, a friend. Picture the conversation as it usually goes: half-turned, glancing at a screen, thinking about the next thing. Now picture it again, with your whole face toward them. Phone down. Eyes up. Listening to the end of the sentence. Notice what changes in the space between you. The bell holds the time.
Keruvim. Cherubim. The two golden figures on the ark, facing each other, with the voice speaking from between them.
Your line: the voice between the faces. Today, in one conversation, face the person fully, phone away, until they've finished speaking. Day three hundred fifty-six.

screen: `DAY 356 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TERUMAH: THE POLES STAY IN (EXODUS 25:15).`

howItsDone: The cherubim are studied in Terumah each year, and the synagogue ark takes its name from the sanctuary's ark; some Jewish teachers use the facing cherubim to speak about presence in marriage, friendship and study partners.
